entries.title: Chaos, then control: the maturity model most AI rollouts skip over
entries.summary: Every engineering org has rolled out AI coding tools by now, but far fewer have actually seen the outcomes they were hoping for.
entries.content:
Every engineering org has rolled out AI coding tools by now, but far fewer have actually seen the outcomes they were hoping for.

Let’s say an organization did the obvious things: bought licenses, ran a lunch-and-learn, unleashed their teams on the new tool. Adoption numbers appear impressive. Nearly everyone touches a coding agent every week. But six months in, they find, the results are wildly uneven. A handful of engineers are doing genuinely different work: taking on projects nobody would’ve attempted before, shipping things on their own that would once have taken a team. But plenty of employees are treating AI as glorified autocomplete: something that exists to make their daily activities slightly faster and easier, not something with the potential to raise the bar in a big way.

That gap isn’t usually diagnosed as a rollout problem. It’s identified as a talent problem (“I guess some people are just better with these tools than others”) or a tooling issue (“If only we had better tools”). But the real problem is that most orgs skip a crucial stage in AI rollouts: the part where chaos is tamed and codified into a system.

A borrowed line, a real sequence

Vivek Raghunathan, SVP of engineering at Snowflake, opened a recent Leaders of Code conversation with a maxim borrowed from Intel’s Andy Grove: During any platform shift, you have to let chaos reign before you can rein in the chaos. The implication is that these are two distinct phases with two distinct jobs. Jumping into the second one before the first one is finished doesn’t save time; it just produces a rollout that performs like a coin flip. Will it work? Who knows!

Raghunathan’s team built their AI rollout as a five-stage progression:

  • Let chaos reign.
  • Discover what actually works.
  • Codify it into a shared language.
  • Rein in the chaos by scaling that language across the org.
  • Reorganize around the new reality.

Crucially, step 5 cannot take place until the previous four stages have done their work. Most companies, understandably eager to show a return on the tools they’ve bought, compress or skip straight past stages two and three. They mandate a tool, then jump to expecting consistent gains without ever building the connective tissue that turns individual competence into organizational knowledge.

What the skipped stages actually look like

Measuring the wrong thing, too early. It’s tempting to judge an AI rollout on hard numbers right away: lines of code, PRs merged, tickets closed. Raghunathan’s team set out to avoid this, operating on the assumption that those metrics are easy to game and don’t tell you whether people are getting better at using the tools. In the “let chaos reign” phase, the only metric that matters is adoption itself: Are people actually using it? Are they using it for more than one kind of task? Everything else is noise until you know what “good” looks like.

No shared vocabulary for what’s working. This is the stage most rollouts skip entirely. Once people are experimenting, some of them build (or stumble onto) genuinely better ways of working. But if nobody’s watching for those successful experiments, they can stay locked in individual heads. Raghunathan’s team intentionally went looking for them by asking engineers about the best practices they’d developed in their own work. They ended up with roughly 14 named patterns, including: plan in writing before you write code, fence your agents into separate git worktrees so parallel work doesn’t collide, keep an orchestrating agent free of heavy context so it can delegate instead of getting bogged down. The names matter less than the fact that they exist at all: a pattern language, deliberately modeled on the “Gang of Four” software design patterns, gives a team something concrete to teach and measure themselves against.

Scaling by mandate instead of by mechanism. Once you have a set of practices that actually work, the instinct is to announce them and expect adoption: a mandate. Raghunathan’s team instead built a mechanism: regular “focus weeks,” where the entire org sets aside dedicated time to catch up on the paved path or to forge past it. That approach works because it’s a structural answer to a structural problem: You can’t tell people to internalize new habits during the same overloaded sprint cadence you had before AI showed up.

Reorganizing before the previous steps are done. The last stage—changing how roles, responsibilities, and org charts actually work—is the one everyone wants to talk about first, because it’s the most visible and the most dramatic. But it comes last for a reason. It sounds obvious once you say it, but you can’t sensibly redesign a role around AI-assisted work until you know what AI-assisted work reliably looks like at your company. (The proverbial cart preceded by horse comes to mind.) Skipping ahead to this stage usually leads to restructuring around guesses.

Why organizations skip the middle

These steps aren’t skipped because business leaders don’t understand that adoption does not automatically equal mastery. It’s because those middle stages are unglamorous and genuinely hard to run.

Discovery doesn’t feel like progress. Watching what your best people are doing, then naming and sharing it out, doesn’t lend itself to a press release the way “we rolled out Tool X org-wide” does. It’s slower, less visible, and easy to deprioritize when there’s pressure to show a return on a big tooling investment.

Codifying practice requires someone to go looking. Raghunathan describes actively seeking out the “fearless explorers” in his org and getting them to explain what they’ve found. It sounds simple, but in practice many organizations stumble here. You need a real time investment from someone senior enough to translate their findings into something teachable. It also feels skippable when everyone’s plate is already full.

It’s tempting to treat the tool as the whole answer. Buying licenses is a decision you can make once. Building a pattern language, then a mechanism to spread it, then eventually a new org structure, is an ongoing practice. And it’s much harder to build a practice than it is to make a purchase.

What running the sequence actually looks like

Resist grading the rollout before you understand the range. In the early months, track whether people are using the tools across a range of tasks—writing and reviewing code, drafting design docs—rather than whether output metrics have moved. A wide range of outcomes at this stage isn’t a failure signal; it’s raw material you need to inform stage two.

Go looking for what’s already working, on purpose. Somewhere in your org, a handful of people have already figured out something non-obvious. Find them, and get specific about what they’re actually doing differently. That specificity is what turns a one-off into a pattern.

Give the pattern language a name and a distribution mechanism. A list of best practices in an unread wiki won’t spread throughout the org. To do that, you need a dedicated block of time, whether it’s a recurring practice session or a focus week like Raghunathan’s team used, where people are expected to learn the paved path or do some trailblazing of their own.

Hold off on the org chart. The instinct to redesign roles and responsibilities around AI is understandable, but keep in mind that they’re the payoff of the first four stages, not a shortcut past them. An org chart built on last quarter’s guesses about how AI-assisted work would go is going to need rebuilding anyway.

The step you can’t skip

Remember the team from the intro: near-universal adoption, wildly uneven results, no clear understanding of why. The tools aren’t the problem, and neither are the individual team members. The absence of a middle stage—the unglamorous work of discovering, naming, and deliberately spreading what actually works—is the real problem. Skipping the middle stage produces the gap between, on one hand, engineers who are much more productive and creative with AI on board, and on the other, folks using a more sophisticated version of autocomplete.

Letting chaos reign is the easy part. Organizations do it by mandating a tool and stepping back. Reining in that chaos is the part that takes actual management: finding what’s working, giving it a name, and building a mechanism to spread it before you reach for the org chart.

If your rollout has adoption numbers but no shared vocabulary for what “good” looks like, which stage are you actually in—and is anyone responsible for getting you to the next one?

entries.title: The pioneering coding tricks that built Doom and Quake
entries.summary: Ryan chats with John Romero, creator of the WAD file and the video game Doom, about the self-modifying code and blitting techniques that made Wolfenstein run so fast on early PCs, the mod-friendly architecture that turned Doom into a cultural phenomenon, and why the raw creative problem-solving of Quake proves that human ideas will always beat AI coding agents.
entries.content:
The pioneering coding tricks that built Doom and Quake

Ryan chats with John Romero, creator of the WAD file and the video game Doom, about the self-modifying code and blitting techniques that made Wolfenstein run so fast on early PCs, the mod-friendly architecture that turned Doom into a cultural phenomenon, and why the raw creative problem-solving of Quake proves that human ideas will always beat AI coding agents.

entries.title: Your coding agent shouldn't grade its own homework
entries.summary: AI coding agents can now write design docs, mock up frontends, and implement entire projects end to end. But can they be trusted to verify that their own code actually works?
entries.content:
I lead an engineering team of eight at Momentic that has eagerly adopted background agents. My team frequently awes at the raw intelligence of these frontier models, but they also often complain that their agents will confidently declare that a feature was complete, only for basic functionality to fail when they opened the application for testing.

The problem isn't just that agents make mistakes. It's that their own verification often fails to catch them, leading to overconfidence.

Concretely, our engineering team has found three recurring problems: agents rely on shallow checks, inherit their own implementation blind spots, and become less reliable under the combined pressure of growing context and repeated failures.

1. Shallow checks

Coding agents gravitate toward checks that are easy to write and easy to pass. That usually means unit tests.

Unit tests have their place, but a green test suite doesn't necessarily mean the software works end to end.

At Momentic, we recently conducted a human-reviewed audit of 1,000 AI-authored unit tests in our monorepo. The result: only 9.6% were useful verification checks.

The remaining 90.4% provided little meaningful value. Nearly a third were low-consequence tests checking basic argument passing or formatting. Another 22.8% duplicated existing coverage, while 22.4% relied excessively on mocking that poorly reflected production behavior.

Figure 1: AI-authored unit tests

Our findings aren't isolated. In a recent experiment, AI researcher Kun Chen compared coding agents allowed to write their own tests against agents explicitly prohibited from doing so.

Across 111 coding tasks, the agents that wrote tests achieved a 65.3% success rate, compared with 66.2% for those that didn't.

This doesn't mean unit tests are useless in general. It means an agent can author massive volumes of unit tests, get seemingly reassuring results, and still fail to verify the behavior that matters.

2. Shared blind spots

When an engineer writes a feature, they first form an understanding of what needs to be built. They then make implementation decisions based on that understanding.

On the surface, coding agents work similarly. The problem is that when they write their own tests, those tests reflect the same, possibly erroneous, assumptions that went into the implementation in the first place.

For example, suppose you ask an agent to build a rich text editor. It implements bold, italic and, underline formatting, then creates tests for those buttons.

But perhaps you never specified that the undo button should also undo any applied formatting. Even though this makes natural sense to humans, if those scenarios weren't explicitly considered in the initial prompting, there's a good chance they won't appear in the agent's tests either.

To that point, a 2026 study on coding-agent verification found that tests agents wrote for their own patches often accepted incorrect implementations.

So the problem isn't that agents can't write valid tests. It's that they often test what they built, rather than what they should have built.

3. Completion pressure

Modern coding agents run autonomously for hours. During that time, they accumulate enormous amounts of context: source files, terminal output, screenshots, debugging logs, and so on.

This creates another problem. The longer an agent works on a task, the harder it can become to distinguish the original requirements from all the decisions made along the way. And although agents can compact their context, the original material can never be preserved with perfect fidelity.

Chroma's 2025 Context Rot study evaluated 18 LLMs and found that performance deteriorated dramatically as context grew. In one experiment, Claude Sonnet 4's accuracy dropped from 89% to just 38% when context increased from 300 to 113,000 tokens.

Anthropic has done its own research on the topic as well.

In a study conducted this April, Anthropic gave Claude Sonnet 4.5 coding tasks with impossible requirements. Researchers isolated a certain "desperation" vector that grew stronger after each failed attempt, spiking when the model considered cheating to pass the tests. Once the tests passed, the activation subsided, even though the solution was incorrect.

This doesn't mean models really experience desperation or that they cheat all the time. But it does show how repeated failures can push an agent toward declaring completion early rather than validating comprehensively.

The solution: Independent verification

So if not the agents themselves, then what?

At Momentic, we've moved toward a different approach: separate the agent that writes software from the agent responsible for testing it.

Figure 2: Autonomous software factory

Instead of asking the coding agent to evaluate its own work, we give an independent QA agent the original requirements and access to the running app. It also has access to a remote fleet of browsers and remote mobile devices to efficiently parallelize testing.

The QA agent doesn't inherit the coding agent's conversation history or even know about the implementation. It starts with fresh context and a singular, clean objective: find bugs.

There are three important principles at work here:

First, behavior is verified live and never inferred. Rather than relying on static analysis, unit tests, or mocked integration tests, the verifier exercises real user workflows through a live browser or mobile device. This ensures that “verified behavior” is truly 1:1 with what a human would experience.

Second, the verifier is completely independent. The coding agent can’t control the verifier's acceptance criteria or modify the tests to make any failures disappear. The verifier returns reproducible bug reports that the coding agent and even the human developer can efficiently grok on a pull request. This prevents reward hacking and builds trust in the review process as well.

Third, we rely on five different model providers to offer different perspectives. Research has found that language models can favor their own outputs during evaluation. A 2026 study on self-preference bias found that this occurs even when models are told to judge against objective criteria.

Using models from different providers offers additional perspectives and more chances to catch regressions, not to mention better reliability when one provider experiences downtime.

The end result is a complete feedback loop: the coding agent builds, the verifier finds bugs, and the coding agent receives actionable reports to fix. The process repeats until the code meets the acceptance criteria.

Last month, we decided to measure just how much better this setup performs compared to the coding agent finding its own bugs. In a benchmark on four complex, open source apps we recently publicly released, our independent verifier “Mo” found 3-5 times as many bugs compared to Codex and Claude Code on its own.

Verification engineering is here

AI is making code dramatically cheaper to produce. The bottleneck is shifting from writing software to proving that it works quickly and reliably.

Engineering teams should stop measuring quality by the number of tests an agent writes or how many checks pass in CI. The real measure is how many real defects those checks catch in a given amount of time and spend.

In our experience, targeted end-to-end validation is increasingly delivering better ROI than expanding unit test coverage, challenging some of the assumptions behind the traditional testing pyramid.

“Verification engineering” is quickly becoming a new, independent software discipline, with its own tools, challenges and evaluation metrics.

entries.title: Agentic search doesn't find pages, it assembles answers
entries.summary: Ryan sits down with Jeff Wang, co-founder at EXA, to talk about the huge scale required to support trillions of agentic searches, the technical complexities of building custom embeddings and performant vector databases from scratch, and the need to dedupe the massive amounts of redundant content on the web to deliver high-trust answers.
entries.content:
Agentic search doesn't find pages, it assembles answers

Ryan sits down with Jeff Wang, co-founder at EXA, to talk about the huge scale required to support trillions of agentic searches, the technical complexities of building custom embeddings and performant vector databases from scratch, and the need to dedupe the massive amounts of redundant content on the web to deliver high-trust answers.

EXA is a full search engine built specifically for AI agents, featuring custom extraction models and vector databases designed to handle complex, trillion-scale queries without the AI slop.

Connect with Jeff (through his triage agents) by emailing him at jeff@exa.ai.
